column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 45: “Allah and His Messenger have forbidden the sale of wine”

column2: From Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, in the year of the Conquest, while he was in Makkah:

“Allah and His Messenger have forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, swine and idols.” It was said: Messenger of Allah, what about the fat of carrion? Ships are coated with it, hides are oiled with it, and people light their lamps with it.

He said: “No; it is unlawful.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said at that point: “May Allah fight the Jews! Allah made the fat unlawful for them, so they melted it down, then sold it and consumed its price.” Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it.
The two of them recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir.
In a narration of Muslim's, Yazīd said: ʿAṭāʾ wrote to me — and he mentioned it. That is why Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said: I do not know that Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb heard anything from ʿAṭāʾ,
meaning that he narrates from him only from his writing. Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb also narrated it from ʿAmr ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbdah, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet ﷺ, in similar terms.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: It reached ʿUmar that a man had sold wine, and he said: May Allah fight him!
Does he not know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “May Allah fight the Jews! The fat was made unlawful for them, so they melted it down and sold it”? In one narration: “and consumed its price.”

Abū Dāwūd recorded something similar from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, adding: “When Allah makes the eating of something unlawful for them, He makes its price unlawful for them.” Ibn Abī Shaybah recorded it, and his wording is: “When Allah makes something unlawful, He makes its price unlawful.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “May Allah fight the Jews! The fat was made unlawful for them, so they sold it and consumed its price.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿĀʾishah, who said: When the verses at the end of Sūrat al-Baqarah were revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out and recited them to the people, and then forbade trade in wine.
In a narration of Muslim's: When the verses at the end of Sūrat al-Baqarah about usury were revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to the mosque and made trade in wine unlawful.
Muslim recorded from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has made wine unlawful; so whoever this verse reaches while he has some of it, let him neither drink it nor sell it.”
He said: So the people brought what they had of it out onto the road of Madīnah and poured it away.

He also recorded from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās that a man gave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a skin of wine as a gift, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: “Did you know that Allah has made it unlawful?”
He said: No. Then he whispered to someone, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: “What did you whisper to him?”
He said: I told him to sell it. He said: “The One who made drinking it unlawful has made selling it unlawful.” So he opened the skins until what was in them had run out.

What all these hadiths amount to is that whatever Allah has made it unlawful to benefit from, it is unlawful to sell and to consume its price, as was stated explicitly in the narration mentioned earlier:
“When Allah makes something unlawful, He makes its price unlawful.” This is a general, comprehensive statement that holds for everything whose intended use is unlawful, and that is of two categories.
The first is what is used while it itself remains intact, such as idols: the use intended of them is associating partners with Allah, which is the greatest of all sins without exception.

With this go things whose use is unlawful, such as books of shirk, sorcery, innovation and misguidance; likewise unlawful images and unlawful instruments of amusement, such as the tanbūr; and likewise buying slave girls for singing.
In the Musnad, from Abū Umāmah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah sent me as a mercy and guidance to the worlds, and commanded me to wipe out pipes and kinnārāt” — meaning

lutes and musical instruments — “and the idols that used to be worshipped in the Jāhiliyyah. My Lord swore by His might: No servant of Mine drinks a mouthful of wine but I will give him to drink in its place of the boiling water of Hell,
whether he is punished or forgiven; and no one gives it to a small child to drink but I will give him to drink in its place of the boiling water of Hell, whether he is punished or forgiven;

and no servant of Mine leaves it out of fear of Me but I will give it to him to drink in the Enclosure of Holiness. Selling them, buying them, teaching them and trading in them are not lawful, and their price is unlawful” — meaning singing girls.

Al-Tirmidhī recorded it, and his wording is: Do not sell singing girls, do not buy them and do not teach them; there is no good in trading in them, and their price is unlawful. It was about the like of this that Allah revealed:

“And among people is one who buys idle talk…” [Luqmān 31:6]. Ibn Mājah also recorded it. There is criticism of the hadith's chain, and something similar has been narrated from the hadith of ʿUmar and of ʿAlī by two chains that also contain weakness.

Those who hold singing to be unlawful, such as Aḥmad and Mālik, say: When a singing slave girl is sold, she is to be sold as an untrained girl, and no price is taken for her singing — even if the slave girl belongs to an orphan; Aḥmad stated this explicitly. Singing does not prevent the sale of a male or female slave as such,
since they can be used for things other than singing, through service and the like, which is among the principal purposes of slaves.
Admittedly, if it is known that the buyer is buying the slave only for the unlawful use, it is not permissible to sell to him, according to Imam Aḥmad and other scholars,

just as, in their view, it is not permissible to sell grape juice to one who will make it into wine, to sell weapons during civil strife, to sell fragrant herbs and drinking cups to one known to drink wine over them, or to sell a slave boy to one known for indecency.
The second category is what is used by being consumed. If the principal use intended of it is unlawful, it is unlawful to sell,

just as it is unlawful to sell swine, wine and carrion, even though some of them have uses that are not unlawful, such as eating carrion in dire need, washing down a morsel one is choking on with wine, and putting out a fire with it,

and, in the view of some, sewing with pig's bristles, and making use of its hair and hide, in the view of those who allow that. But since these uses are not the ones intended, no account was taken of them, and sale was made unlawful because the principal use intended of swine and carrion is eating them, and of wine drinking it;

no attention was paid to anything else. He ﷺ pointed to this meaning when it was said to him, “What about the fat of carrion? Ships are coated with it, hides are oiled with it, and people light their lamps with it,” and he said: “No; it is unlawful.”

People have differed over the interpretation of his words ﷺ, “It is unlawful.” One group said: He meant that this use of the fat of carrion is unlawful; that would then reinforce the prohibition of selling carrion, since he did not make any use of it permissible.

Another group said: Rather, he meant that selling it is unlawful, even though it may be used in these ways; but the principal intended use of fat is eating, so selling it is not permissible for that reason.

The scholars have differed over making use of the fat of carrion. ʿAṭāʾ allowed it, and Ibn Manṣūr transmitted the same from Aḥmad and Isḥāq, except that Isḥāq said: When there is need for it; but if one can do without it,

then no. Aḥmad said: It is permissible if he does not touch it with his hand. Another group said that it is not permissible; this is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr related it as the consensus of all but ʿAṭāʾ.

As for pure oils that have become impure through some filth falling into them, there is a well-known disagreement in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and others over whether they may be used for lighting lamps and the like; and there are two reported positions of Aḥmad on it.
As for selling them, most scholars hold that it is not permissible. There is a reported position of Aḥmad that they may be sold to a disbeliever, who is told that they are impure;

this is narrated from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. Some of the scholars of our school derived the permissibility of selling them from the permissibility of using them for lamps; but this is weak, and contrary to Aḥmad's explicit statement distinguishing the two,

for the fat of carrion may not be sold even if it is held permissible to use it. Others derived it from the view that such oils are purified by washing, in which case they would be like a garment smeared with filth.
The apparent sense of Aḥmad's words is that selling them is prohibited absolutely,
for he gave as his reason that impure oil has carrion in it, and the price of carrion is not to be consumed.
As for the other parts of carrion, whatever of them is judged pure may be sold, since it may be used: such as hair and horn, according to those who hold them pure,

and likewise the hide, according to those who hold that it is pure without tanning, as is related from al-Zuhrī; al-Bukhārī's chapter heading points to this, and he argued from his words: “Only the eating of carrion is unlawful.”
As for the majority, who hold that the hide is impure before tanning, most of them forbade selling it at that stage,

since it is part of the carrion. Some took an isolated view and permitted selling it, like an impure garment; but the garment is pure and filth has come upon it, while the hide of carrion is part of it and impure in itself.
Sālim ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said: Is selling the hides of carrion anything other than eating its flesh?
Ṭāwūs and ʿIkrimah disliked it, and al-Nakhaʿī said: They used to dislike selling them and consuming their price.
Once they are tanned, those who hold that tanning purifies them permit selling them, and those who do not hold that it purifies them do not.

Aḥmad stated explicitly that wheat with donkey's urine on it may not be sold until it is washed; perhaps he meant selling it to someone unaware of its state, for fear that he might eat it without knowing it is impure.
As for the dog, it is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the price of a dog.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “The worst of earnings are the earnings of a prostitute, the price of a dog and the earnings of a cupper.”
It also has, from Maʿqil al-Jazarī, from Abū al-Zubayr, who said: I asked Jābir about the price of a dog and a cat, and he said: The Prophet ﷺ rebuked people for that.
This is known only from Ibn Lahīʿah, from Abū al-Zubayr.

Imam Aḥmad regarded Maʿqil's narrations from Abū al-Zubayr as munkar (objectionable), saying: They resemble the hadiths of Ibn Lahīʿah. This has been looked into and found to be as Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said.

The scholars have differed over selling a dog. Most of them held it unlawful, among them al-Awzāʿī, Mālik in his well-known position, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and others. Abū Hurayrah said: It is ill-gotten gain (suḥt). Ibn Sīrīn said: It is the foulest of earnings.
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā said: I do not care whether I consume the price of a dog or the price of a pig.
These scholars have several lines of reasoning.

First, that selling dogs was forbidden only because of their impurity. These held that the sale of everything impure in itself is unlawful; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn Jarīr, and a number of the scholars of our school agreed with them,

such as Ibn ʿAqīl in his Naẓariyyāt, and others. They were forced to hold that we may permit the sale of the mule and the donkey only if we do not hold them impure; and this goes against the consensus.

Second, that the dog was not made permissible to use and keep without restriction, as the mule and the donkey are; keeping it is permitted only for specific needs, and that does not make selling it permissible, just as dire need for carrion and blood does not make selling them permissible. This is the line of reasoning of a group of the scholars of our school and others.
Third, that selling it was forbidden only because of its lowness and contemptibility: it has no value except to the miserly and base, and it is easily found;

so taking its price was forbidden to encourage sharing whatever one has of it beyond one's needs. This is the line of reasoning of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others of the Salaf, and some of the scholars of our school said the same of the prohibition of selling cats.

A group allowed selling those dogs that may be kept, such as hunting dogs. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah and his followers, and a reported position of Mālik. They said: What was forbidden was only the sale of those that may not be kept.
Ḥammād ibn Salamah narrated from Abū al-Zubayr, from Jābir, that the Prophet ﷺ forbade the price of a dog and a cat, except for a hunting dog. Al-Nasāʾī recorded it and said:

It is a munkar hadith. He also said: It is not authentic. Al-Dāraquṭnī mentioned that the correct version is mawqūf on Jābir (his own words). Aḥmad said: No allowance for the hunting dog is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ.
Al-Bayhaqī and others indicated that this exception confused some of the narrators, who took it as referring to sale, when it actually refers to keeping.
Ḥammād ibn Salamah is not strong in his narrations from Abū al-Zubayr, and whoever says that this hadith meets Muslim's conditions — as a group of later scholars have supposed — is mistaken,
for Muslim recorded nothing from Ḥammād ibn Salamah from Abū al-Zubayr, and he made clear in his book al-Tamyīz that Ḥammād's narrations from many of his shaykhs, or most of them, are not strong.
As for selling a cat, the scholars have differed over whether it is disliked. Some disliked it; this is narrated from Abū Hurayrah, Jābir, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid,
Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Awzāʿī, and Aḥmad in one reported position, who said: It is less serious than selling the skins of beasts of prey. This is the choice of Abū Bakr among the scholars of our school.

Selling cats was allowed by Ibn ʿAbbās, by ʿAṭāʾ in one report, and by al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, al-Ḥakam and Ḥammād; it is the view of al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, and of Aḥmad in his well-known position. There are two reports from Isḥāq. It is reported of al-Ḥasan that he disliked selling them but allowed buying them in order to make use of them.
Some of these did not consider the prohibition of selling them authentic. Aḥmad said: I know of nothing on it that is established or authentic. He also said: The hadiths on it are confused.
Some took the prohibition to apply to cats of no use, such as wild cats and the like.
Others said: He forbade selling them only

because it is mean and shows a lack of decency: they are easily found and there is a pressing need for them, so they are among the conveniences of people, whose surplus costs nothing to give away, and being miserly with that is among the ugliest of blameworthy traits. That is why he rebuked people for taking their price.

As for the other animals that are not eaten, those of no use, such as insects and the like, may not be sold. Whatever use is mentioned for some of them is slight, and so does not make selling them permissible,

just as the Prophet ﷺ did not permit selling carrion when the uses it had were mentioned to him. That is why the correct view is that it is not permissible to sell leeches for sucking blood, worms for fishing, and the like.

As for those that are useful for hunting, such as the cheetah, the hawk and the falcon, most of the scholars of our school relate two reported positions of Aḥmad on whether they may be sold. Some of them permitted selling them, mentioned that there is consensus on it and explained away the report of dislike; among them is al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā in al-Mujarrad.

Others said that it is not permissible to sell the cheetah or the vulture, relating another view that it is permissible, while permitting the sale of hawks and falcons without relating any disagreement; this is the view of Ibn Abī Mūsā.

Most scholars permitted selling the falcon, the hawk, the eagle and the like, among them al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Shāfiʿī and Isḥāq. What is explicitly reported from Aḥmad in most of the narrations from him is that selling them is permissible;

in one reported position he withheld judgement on whether it is permissible when they are untrained. Al-Khallāl said: The position acted upon is what the majority narrated: that selling them is permissible in every case.

Some of the scholars of our school gave the elephant the same ruling as the cheetah and the like, but this is open to question. What is explicitly reported from Aḥmad in the narration of Ḥanbal is that it is not lawful to sell or buy it;
he treated it like a beast of prey. It is related that al-Ḥasan said: Its back is not to be ridden; and he said: It is a transformed creature. All of this indicates that there is no benefit in it.

It is not permissible to sell a bear; al-Qāḍī said so in al-Mujarrad. Ibn Abī Mūsā said: It is not permissible to sell a monkey; and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I know of no disagreement among the scholars on this. Al-Qāḍī said in al-Mujarrad:

If it is of use somewhere, for guarding goods, it is like the falcon and the hawk; otherwise it is like the lion, and may not be sold. The correct view is that it is prohibited absolutely: this use is slight and not what it is intended for, so it does not make selling it permissible, like the uses of carrion.

Among the things whose sale is forbidden are the corpses of disbelievers when they are killed. Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: On the day of the Trench the Muslims killed a man of the idolaters,
and the idolaters offered money for his corpse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Hand his corpse over to them, for it is a foul corpse and a foul blood price,” and he accepted nothing from them.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded it, and his wording is: The idolaters wanted to buy the body of a man of the idolaters, and the Prophet ﷺ refused to sell it to them.
Wakīʿ recorded it in his book by another route, from ʿIkrimah, in mursal form; then Wakīʿ said: A corpse is not to be sold.
Ḥarb said: I said to Isḥāq: What do you say about selling the corpses of idolaters to idolaters? He said: No.

Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī narrated that al-Mustawrid al-ʿIjlī, who had become a Christian, was brought to ʿAlī. He called on him to repent, and when he refused, he killed him. The Christians asked for his corpse for thirty thousand, but ʿAlī refused and burned it.
